We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1624)
response:
Continual learning systems must acquire new tasks sequentially without degrading performance on prior ones — the core failure mode being catastrophic interference, where new gradient updates overwrite weights that encode old knowledge. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures seem like a natural fix: if different experts specialize for different tasks, updates to one expert shouldn't corrupt another. The critical complication is asymmetric expert utilization — routing mechanisms (typically softmax-based top-k gates) don't distribute inputs uniformly, so a small subset of experts becomes a bottleneck handling most tokens while others remain underutilized or "dead." The expert worries that sparsity, rather than providing protective isolation, can actually concentrate interference: if two tasks both route disproportionately to the same dominant expert, you've recreated the overwriting problem but now hidden it behind an architecture that looks like it should be safe. Worse, the routing function itself is a shared, dense component that adapts continuously, meaning task-specific routing patterns from earlier tasks get silently corrupted even when the expert weights are frozen — a failure mode beginners never check for because it's invisible in standard accuracy metrics until a significant regression appears.

The destructiveness of interference is primarily determined by the directional alignment of gradient updates in parameter space: if the gradient for task B lies in a subspace orthogonal to the gradient for task A, updates can coexist with minimal overwriting, but if they're nearly collinear (pointing in opposite or similar directions through the same weight dimensions), interference is severe regardless of magnitude. This is formalized in the gradient interference metric used in works like Gradient Episodic Memory (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017), which measures the dot product of new-task gradients against old-task gradients — negative dot products signal destructive interference. The curvature of the loss landscape around expert weights matters too: a flat direction (low Hessian eigenvalue) can absorb new updates without displacing old minima, while sharp directions get overwritten catastrophically, which is why EWC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) uses Fisher information as a proxy for curvature to penalize updates in high-curvature dimensions. Sparsity changes this geometry in a non-obvious way: when only the top-k experts receive gradients per forward pass, the effective gradient is blocked-sparse — most expert weight matrices receive zero gradient — which sounds protective but actually concentrates the full curvature problem into the narrow set of active experts, dramatically raising the Hessian eigenvalues in those experts' parameter subspaces. Empirically, in Switch Transformer-style routing (Fedus et al., 2022) with top-1 gating, load imbalance of 10:1 across experts means a single expert's weights see roughly 10× the gradient variance of a balanced system, compressing what should be distributed interference into a much smaller manifold. The beginner assumes sparsity lowers interference globally; the expert sees it as a variance concentrator that makes the collision, when it happens, geometrically worse than in a dense network.

If you freeze the expert weights after task A and only allow the router to adapt for task B, under what conditions does router-only adaptation still produce interference — and what does that reveal about where task identity is actually encoded in an MoE?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1626)
response:
Router-only adaptation still produces interference when task B's optimal routing distribution requires expert combinations that are geometrically incompatible with task A's learned representations — specifically, when the input embeddings for task B activate routing logits that, after softmax, assign high probability to experts whose internal weight structure was shaped exclusively by task A's data distribution, meaning the frozen expert outputs are mismatched to task B's needs regardless of how the router combines them. This reveals that task identity in an MoE is jointly encoded across both the routing function and the expert weights, not cleanly separable — the router learns to send inputs to experts whose weights have co-adapted to produce useful representations for that routing decision, so freezing weights breaks the co-adaptation contract. Concretely, in the ST-MoE experiments (Zoph et al., 2022), fine-tuning only routing parameters on downstream tasks recovered substantially less performance than full fine-tuning, with the gap widening on tasks distributionally distant from pretraining — a direct signature of this co-adaptation dependency. A subtler interference mechanism appears when task B's router updates shift the token-to-expert assignment distribution globally: even for task A inputs seen at inference, the router now sends them to different experts than during training, effectively corrupting task A's performance without touching a single expert weight — this is interference through routing drift rather than weight overwriting. This implies that task identity is encoded in the routing trajectory — the dynamic path an input takes through the expert graph — not just in static weight values, which is why methods like task-specific routing masks (as explored in DSelect-k, Hazimeh et al., 2021) attempt to make routing decisions non-interfering by construction rather than relying on weight isolation alone. The deep implication is that any continual learning strategy for MoEs that only protects expert weights while leaving the router fully plastic has misidentified where the knowledge lives.

prompt:
Since routing drift can corrupt task A even with frozen expert weights, what would a minimally invasive mechanism look like that stabilizes routing for old tasks without preventing the router from learning useful new assignments — and is there a fundamental tradeoff between those two objectives?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1627)
response:
The minimally invasive approach is to treat routing stabilization as a conditional constraint rather than a weight penalty: store a small replay buffer of task A inputs, compute their routing distributions periodically, and add a KL-divergence term to the loss that penalizes deviation from those stored distributions — this is essentially applying the continual learning distillation idea (as in LwF, Li & Hoiem, 2017) specifically to router logits rather than output predictions. A more surgical variant freezes only the routing decision boundaries for high-confidence task A inputs (those where the top-1 expert received >0.9 softmax probability) while leaving low-confidence routing decisions plastic, exploiting the observation that high-confidence routes are most load-bearing for task A performance and most vulnerable to drift. The fundamental tradeoff is real and has a clean information-theoretic framing: the router is a shared bottleneck that must compress task identity signals from inputs into discrete expert assignments, and stabilizing its behavior for task A's input manifold necessarily constrains the representational capacity available for task B's routing, with the severity scaling with the overlap between task input distributions in the router's embedding space. When tasks are distributionally distant (e.g., code generation vs. sentiment classification), their inputs occupy nearly disjoint regions of the router's input space, so stabilization constraints are nearly non-binding and the tradeoff is mild — but when tasks share surface features with different deep structure (e.g., two domains of scientific text), the router cannot easily distinguish them, and stabilizing one routing pattern actively impedes learning the other. Empirically, PackNet-style progressive freezing (Mallya & Lazebnik, 2018), though designed for dense networks, suggests that ~60-80% of routing capacity can be stabilized before new-task learning degrades meaningfully, but this number is architecture-dependent and collapses badly under high expert utilization asymmetry because the "available" capacity is not uniformly distributed — it's concentrated in underutilized experts that may be structurally mismatched to new tasks. The honest answer is that the tradeoff is unavoidable when tasks collide in router input space, and minimally invasive mechanisms buy time rather than eliminate the problem — the real solution requires either input-space separation (task tokens, prompt prefixes) or a router architecture that can represent multiple stable routing functions simultaneously.

Implicit task inference fails most severely under distributional ambiguity — when the surface statistics of an input are consistent with multiple tasks the model has learned, a condition that arises concretely when tasks share vocabulary, syntax, or domain but differ in the required computation (e.g., a grammatically well-formed sentence that could be a translation input, a summarization source, or a sentiment target). The failure mode in expert utilization is characteristically bimodal routing collapse: the router, uncertain about task identity, hedges by splitting probability mass across experts associated with competing tasks rather than committing to either, producing a utilization pattern where no expert receives confident assignment and the effective computation is an interpolation between task-specific functions that serves neither task well — this is measurable as a spike in router entropy without a corresponding drop in load imbalance. A second failure condition is task boundary ambiguity during streaming inference, where early tokens in a sequence are statistically consistent with task A but later tokens reveal task B; because top-k routing decisions are made token-by-token without lookahead, early tokens get routed to task A's experts, poisoning the key-value context that later tokens build on — a sequential interference mechanism distinct from weight overwriting. In sparse upcycled models (Komatsuzaki et al., 2023), where dense pretrained weights are split into experts post-hoc, this failure is especially acute because experts never developed strongly differentiated specializations during pretraining, so the router's implicit task signal is weak from the start and inference-time task ambiguity produces nearly uniform expert utilization — the signature of a router that has given up discriminating. Critically, uniform utilization at inference looks deceptively healthy by load-balancing metrics (which typically reward uniformity during training) but is pathological here because it signals inference-time task confusion rather than efficient resource use — a beginner reading utilization logs would misdiagnose the problem as the system working correctly. The deeper issue is that implicit task inference requires the router to solve what is essentially an online clustering problem from limited context, and the MoE architecture provides no explicit mechanism for this; without it, ambiguous inputs don't fail loudly but silently degrade into averaged, blurred computations whose errors only surface in downstream task metrics.

What makes this bound practically important is that it is architecture-independent: no matter how you implement the router — attention-based, MLP, sparse, dense — you cannot route below the mutual information cost of task inference, which means the field's search for clever routing mechanisms is subject to a fundamental ceiling that has not been explicitly acknowledged in the continual learning MoE literature.
